title: If BERA Has Confidence in These Impossible Articles Why Should We Have Confidence in BERA
author: Stephen Vainker
summary: Vainker documents 10 specific BERA-published papers — all flagged as likely AI-authored — that BERA investigated and chose to leave standing despite containing what he argues are major errors under COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) guidelines. The errors fall into two categories: incorrect citations and references, and methodologically impossible research designs. In the citations category, papers cite the wrong Roscoe (a marketing journal article instead of a research methods textbook), use a sound-segregation study to support a claim about racial segregation, split a single reference into multiple fictitious co-authors, and include a phrase praising a website 'with just one click' — language no academic would write. In the methods category, papers describe pen-and-paper questionnaires during online lockdown classes, voluntary participation with 100% response rates, the same paragraph repeated three times in succession, and sample arithmetic that is numerically impossible. Vainker's conclusion is institutional: BERA needs to retract these papers, acknowledge the systemic nature of the problem, and stop trying to minimize it, because the alternative is total loss of credibility when journalists eventually cover the story.
points: Incorrect citation as AI signature: multiple papers cite a 'Roscoe' reference, but AI matched the author surname to the wrong Roscoe — a marketing article rather than the correct research-methods textbook — in a way no human who had read either source would do.

Subject-term confusion as AI signature: one paper uses a study about sound segregation (distinguishing sounds) to support a claim about racial/ethnic segregation — because an LLM connected the term 'segregation' without understanding the semantic distinction, an error no human who read the source could make.

Methodological impossibilities include: pen-and-paper questionnaires during online lockdown classes; voluntary participation studies with 100% response rates (logically impossible unless participation was compulsory); and descriptions of a research step that the published paper never actually contains.

Repeated-paragraph bug: one paper's methods section repeats the same paragraph three times consecutively — a characteristic AI generation artifact when the model loops on a section — and BERA found no grounds for retraction.

Vainker's institutional prescription: BERA must draw a clear line between its past and its future, acknowledge the systemic problem, complete retractions across all four journals, and stop making false claims about having independently uncovered the problem or about COPE guidelines not requiring retraction for undisclosed AI authorship.
quotes: BERA must stop digging. Last week, it finally took action to stem the tide of AI-authored garbage in its journals by retracting 19 papers from the British Educational Research Journal. I showed that the retraction notice contained two huge mistakes.
This is not a human error, and means that AI was generating the citations/references. [on the wrong Roscoe citation — a marketing journal article substituted for a research methods textbook]

This paper on ethnic clustering (related to racial segregation) uses a reference on sound segregation (the ability to distinguish between sounds) to justify the claim. This is not a human error — it's clearly AI making a false association based on the term 'segregation,' and the authors have not picked up on it.

In the study, 'a total of 1015 college students completed a pen-and-paper questionnaire in online classes.' Why would you do a pen-and-paper questionnaire in an online class? The participants completed all assessments under the guidance of professionally trained psychology instructors in a calm and controlled environment. If it's an online class, and during lockdown, how is it possible to create this controlled environment?
Lauding a particular website in this way is simply not a sentence any academic would write, particularly the phrase 'with just one click.'
It is an unavoidable fact that BERA has published a lot of low-quality AI-authored articles over the past few years. So far, it has only retracted some papers from one journal.

By making false claims crediting itself with uncovering the problem, completely misrepresenting the COPE guidelines, and taking no action on obviously unsupportable articles, BERA is failing to draw such a line. This will mean, sadly, that BERA will lose all credibility and will do so soon.
